rows.title: Swing-Axle Rear Suspension 'Jacks' and Snaps Into Lift-Off Oversteer

rows.title: Structural Rust in Outriggers, Jacking Points, and Cab Floor
rows.howToFix: Cut out and weld in proper pressed-steel repair sections rather than plating over rot: front outrigger and jacking-point sections, lower cab-floor/bulkhead repair panels, and inner/outer sill sections are all reproduced (Heritage, Bus Depot, etc.). rows.title: All-drum brakes that fade — no stopping power for the way it's driven today
rows.howToFix: The proven bulletproofing upgrade is a bolt-on front disc-brake conversion. Kits exist for both the early link-pin/king-pin spindles (1960-1965) and the later ball-joint spindles, and they bolt to the stock spindle with new rotors, calipers and pads for a dramatic gain in stopping power and fade resistance. Restorers pair the discs with a dual-circuit (tandem) master cylinder for fail-safe braking, all-new braided/quality flex hoses and steel lines, fresh wheel cylinders/seals on the retained rear drums, and a full bleed with DOT-4 fluid. Choose a kit that keeps factory steering geometry (zero-offset/wide-5 or the correct lug pattern for your wheels). The result stops like a modern small car and is the most common safety upgrade on a driven Ghia.

The bulletproofing move is to relocate or properly seal the battery (acid-resistant tray + sealed box) so it can't eat the new pan, and to undercoat the finished underside with a flexible rubberised coating over epoxy primer. rows.title: Heater channel and sill rot — the structural rust that totals Ghia bodies
rows.howToFix: Bite the bullet and replace the full heater channel rather than patching — quality reproduction left/right channels are now available (they were once impossible to source). Restorers brace the body across the door apertures and to a rotisserie or jig BEFORE cutting the old channel out so the shell doesn't sag, replace the channel as a complete unit (not piecemeal), and reinstate the floor-pan-to-channel and front/rear closing-panel seams with seam sealer. The proven bulletproofing step is to weld in epoxy-primed (not just painted) steel, then flood the finished sealed channel with cavity wax (Dynax/Waxoyl) through the heat-duct holes so it never rots from the inside again. Reinstate the rubber duct grommets so warm air still reaches the cabin. Budget for skilled MIG welding and panel alignment; this is the single biggest job on a Ghia restoration.

rows.title: Points-and-condenser ignition that strands you, plus weak 6V electrics
rows.howToFix: Convert the distributor to a drop-in electronic ignition (PerTronix Ignitor or equivalent Hall-effect module in the original-look distributor) to eliminate points and condenser entirely — no more dwell drift, fewer no-starts, and a stronger spark for easier cold starting. Pair it with a coil of the correct resistance (3-4.2 ohm, or add a ballast). On 6V cars, do the well-trodden 6V-to-12V conversion: 12V alternator (55A is plenty for stock) on its stand to replace the generator + regulator, plus 12V coil, bulbs, flasher relay, wiper motor and battery — this transforms cranking, charging at idle, and lighting and makes spares trivial to buy. While the harness is accessible, restorers replace brittle cloth wiring and clean/upgrade the chassis grounds, which fixes a huge share of 'gremlin' faults.

rows.title: Swing-axle rear suspension oversteer and rear-wheel tuck
rows.howToFix: You don't have to convert to IRS to make a swing-axle Ghia safe — the classic bulletproofing combo is a rear camber compensator (a transverse leaf under the gearbox that resists wheel tuck and stabilises rear camber), a front anti-roll/sway bar to dial out understeer balance, and fresh quality gas shocks (e.g. Bilstein/KYB) all round. Restorers also renew the rear axle boots and wheel bearings, set a mild negative rear camber, and run a slightly higher front-than-rear stance to manage weight transfer. For owners who want the best handling, the documented upgrade is to swap to the post-1968 IRS rear (CV-jointed double-jointed axles on trailing arms), which eliminates the camber-change geometry entirely — a bigger job involving an IRS transaxle, trailing arms and spring plates.

rows.title: Worn link-pin / king-pin front beam — vague steering and uneven tyre wear
rows.howToFix: Rebuild or replace as a complete beam. The thorough restorer's route is to strip the beam and fit new king pins, link pins, bronze bushes, thrust washers, seals and torsion-leaf bushes (reaming the new bushes to fit), regrease, and reinstate a strict grease schedule via the zerk fittings. Many builders instead swap the whole beam to a rebuilt ball-joint front end (the maintenance-free joint VW itself adopted for 1966), which is a popular bulletproofing/upgrade path and pairs naturally with a disc-brake conversion; adjustable beams also allow ride-height tuning. Finish with a fresh steering damper, rebuilt or replaced steering box, new tie-rod ends, and a proper front-end alignment to kill the tyre wear.
